title: Hybrid DNS stub-domains and VPC failover - POC notes
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working note for a small customer POC exploring hybrid DNS "stub domain" approaches combined with VPC-level failover for Redwood Private deployments. The customer requirement: run inference nodes in Customer VPC (primary), with Redwood-managed fallbacks (secondary) in our Dedicated region when customer on-prem/VPC connectivity is degraded. They want predictable ingress/egress, no public endpoints for model serving, and DNS-based automatic switchover without manual operator intervention.

Goals (POC success criteria):
- Demonstrate DNS-driven failover that switches traffic to Redwood-managed endpoints within 30s–60s of detected failure.
- Preserve tenant isolation and auditability: all fallback traffic is logged and correlated to tenant id.
- Avoid asymmetric routing and preserve source-IP expectations (where possible) so the customer nets and firewalls don't break sessions.
- Provide a small operator runbook and an automated health-check + failover test harness.

High-level architecture options considered:
1) Conditional forwarder + stub domain (preferred for POC)
   - Customer retains their authoritative internal zone (e.g. internal.customer.local).
   - Customer DNS resolvers are configured with a stub domain for *.inference.customer.internal that forwards to Redwood DNS resolvers for the tenant-specific subdomain.
   - Redwood returns either private IP(s) in customer's VPC (via VPC Endpoint IPs) or addresses for Dedicated fallback (private ips in Redwood-managed VPC) based on health gating.
   - Failover implemented at Redwood DNS layer (health checks + query policy).
   - Pros: clean split-horizon, minimal change to app logic, fast switchover.
   - Cons: requires customer to allow outbound DNS forwarders to Redwood resolvers (TLS/port 853 preferred), and inbound firewall rules to accept fallback IPs.

2) Split-horizon at customer's DNS (pull model)
   - Customer DNS hosts both primary and fallback records and toggles via its health monitors.
   - Pros: customer retains full control, no external DNS dependency.
   - Cons: operationally heavy for customers; exposes more internal knowledge to ops teams.

3) Anycast + global LB in-front with health-based routing
   - Redwood advertises anycast IPs; traffic routed to nearest healthy POP.
   - Pros: simple from customer perspective (single destination IP), avoids DNS complexities.
   - Cons: not acceptable to many regulated customers (anycast/public), and breaks the no-public-endpoint constraint.

Design decisions for POC:
- Use Option 1 (stub domain + Redwood authoritative subdomain). This minimizes customer changes while keeping failover logic centralized at Redwood.
- Use DNS-over-TLS (DoT) or DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) for stub-forwarding to minimize MITM concerns.
- Redwood will provide per-tenant resolver endpoints and an IAM token for TLS mutual auth to avoid abuse.
- Health checks: active TCP/HTTP checks from multiple Redwood vantage points plus synthetic inference request (small model/seq len) to validate service and KV cache warming.
- TTL strategy: set short TTLs (15s–30s) on fallback-critical records and use DNS negative caching guidance to minimize stale state.

Networking details (customer-facing constraints):
- Primary path: customer VPC private endpoint (interface endpoint) with security group allowing traffic from customer subnets.
- Fallback path: Redwood-managed VPC private endpoint with AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint) in customer account OR a cross-account VPC peering/transit attachment depending on customer preference and cloud provider.
- If PrivateLink in customer's account is used, endpoint target is a Redwood ENI in the customer's account; logs are available in customer VPC flow logs + Redwood observability.
- For peering/transit designs, we provide IP ranges for fallback subnets — customer must add route table entries for those ranges and SG/NACL rules to allow the necessary ports (TLS 443, health-check ports).

DNS mapping plan (example):
- Tenant service name: model-v1.tid-123.inference.customer.internal
- When primary healthy -> resolves to 10.32.12.45 (customer private endpoint IP)
- When failed -> resolves to 10.200.5.23 (Redwood fallback IP in ridge-region-a)
- TTL: 20s on both records; CNAMEs used inside Redwood to reduce endpoint churn across rollouts.

Failover mechanics and circuit breaker:
- Health monitors mark primary unhealthy if: 3 consecutive synthetic request failures OR avg latency > SLO for 60s OR missing KV cache handshake.
- Once unhealthy detected, Redwood authoritative returns fallback IPs and emits event to customer audit stream (webhook + console).
- Circuit breaker: attempt to mark primary healthy again only after a prolonged probe period (2 mins), and only if synthetic checks are green for 3 consecutive probes.
- During failover we avoid split-brain by requiring a quorum of vantage points to agree (3/5) before switching.

Security and least-privilege considerations:
- Mutual TLS for any inter-resolver forwarding. Use customer-managed CA or Redwood-provisioned short-lived certs.
- PrivateLink option preferred for zero-public-surface. If not possible, enable policying on fallback ENIs and source-IP allowlists.
- Audit: all fallback requests must include tenant id in a header X-Tenant-ID + signed JWT assertion from customer's gateway (optional). We will log both header and resolved-source-ip on the Redwood side.

Testing plan for the POC:
- Phase 1 (lab): emulated customer VPC inside our test account, stub-forwarder configured, validate healthy->fallback transitions with simulated packet blackhole. Tests: DNS TTL expiry, DoT fallback, mutli-vantage consensus, session affinity degradation.
- Phase 2 (customer staging): deploy PrivateLink endpoint in customer staging VPC, run load tests (1k rps small seq), intentionally block port on primary endpoint and measure switchover time and error rates.
- Phase 3 (post-POC hardening): run 24h chaos window to observe flapping handling and cost impact analysis for fallback traffic.

Operational runbook excerpt (quick steps):
1) Confirm stub domain configured on customer resolvers: dig +tcp @<customer-resolver> model-v1.tid-123.inference.customer.internal
2) Check Redwood health dashboard: /console/tenants/tid-123/health
3) Trigger manual failover (for test): POST /internal/tenants/tid-123/force-failover with auth token
4) Revert: ensure primary probes are green, then POST /internal/tenants/tid-123/clear-failover

Open questions / risks:
- Some customers will not allow any external DNS forwarders. For them we need documented split-horizon templates or an out-of-band control plane integration (API call for record toggle).
- Source-IP preservation for TCP connections: when traffic goes through Redwood fallback path it may NAT source IP -> breaks some firewalls. Need to offer an option to preserve source-IP via GRE / transit (complex) or document required firewall adjustments.
- Cost implications: fallback traffic billed differently; need to solidify billing labels/metrics for customer visibility.
- IPv6: customer's VPCs sometimes prefer v6; PrivateLink fallback via IPv6 is limited. Evaluate per-cloud support.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- Arjun: prototype Redwood authoritative resolver logic + health consensus engine (PR/branch SE-4823) - due 2024-12-01
- Sofia: build lab infra and test harness (Terraform modules, test runner) - due 2024-12-15
- Ethan: draft customer stub-forwarder config guides (AWS Route53 Resolver, Azure DNS forwarding rules) - due 2024-12-08
- Ruth: prepare security checklist and KMS cert rotation pattern for DoT mutual auth - due 2024-12-20

Notes to self:
- Keep TTLs deliberately short for POC but propose 60s for production with additional session draining techniques.
- Record forensic logs during failover window for at least 7 days by default for POC tenants.

Slack threads / references: #se-private-deploy (thread: hybrid-dns-poC), link to confluence above for pattern diagrams.

End of doc (working draft).
